content:
Quick answer: To sleep better with arthritis, ease pain and stiffness before bed (a warm shower or wheat bag for stiffness, a cool pack earlier if a joint is hot), support painful joints with pillows, keep regular bed and wake times, and keep gentle movement in the day. Ask your GP about medicine timing, and get checked if you snore loudly, gasp at night or your mood is dropping.

Broken nights are one of the most common things people with arthritis tell us about. Pain wakes you, stiffness makes turning over hard, and a bad night makes the next day's pain and tiredness feel louder. The good news is that small, steady changes usually help more than buying one expensive gadget. This UK guide covers what to try tonight and when to ask for help.

Why arthritis can disturb sleep

  • Night pain — joints ache when you are still, and inflammatory arthritis can be worse overnight and early morning
  • Stiffness — turning over or getting up for the toilet can be painful
  • Position — lying on a painful hip, shoulder or knee
  • Medicines — for example steroids taken late in the day can keep some people awake; never change a prescription without advice
  • Worry and low mood — common with long-term pain, and they feed poor sleep (see our arthritis and mental health guide)

Tonight: settle pain before bed

  1. Warmth for stiffness — a warm shower, bath or wheat bag 20–30 minutes before bed. Do not sleep on an electric heat pad.
  2. Cool for a hot, swollen joint — a wrapped cold pack for 10–15 minutes earlier in the evening.
  3. Gentle range-of-motion — a few slow movements for stiff joints from the exercise hub, not a hard workout.
  4. Medicine timing — ask your GP or pharmacist whether the timing of your usual pain relief suits your nights. Our pain relief guide explains the options.

Positions and pillows by joint

  • Knee — a pillow between the knees on your side, or a thin pillow under the knees on your back
  • Hip — lie on the less painful side with a pillow between the knees; a mattress topper can ease pressure
  • Back — on your back with a pillow under the knees, or on your side with knees slightly bent
  • Shoulder — avoid lying on the sore side; hug a pillow to rest the arm
  • Hands — ask your physiotherapist or OT whether a resting splint would help

There is no single "best arthritis mattress". Most people do well with something supportive that does not sag; try a topper before replacing a whole bed.

Daytime habits that change your nights

  • Get up at the same time each day, even after a poor night
  • Keep gentle movement in the day — short walks or seated routines often help sleep more than long naps
  • Pace activity so you are not exhausted and wired at bedtime — see pacing and energy management
  • Cut caffeine after early afternoon and keep alcohol low; it can wake you later in the night
  • Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and comfortably cool

If tiredness hangs on even after better nights, read our arthritis fatigue guide, because fatigue often needs more than sleep alone.

Waking in pain at 3am

Keep a glass of water and anything you need within reach. Change position slowly, do a few ankle and knee bends under the covers, and use a calm breathing routine rather than checking your phone. If you are awake for a long stretch, get up, sit somewhere dim and return when sleepy. If night pain is new, severe, or comes with a hot swollen joint, follow the flare-up guide or our flare action plan.

When to see your GP

  • Poor sleep most nights for more than a few weeks despite these steps — ask about CBT for insomnia (CBT-I), which the NHS recommends ahead of sleeping tablets
  • Loud snoring, gasping or stopping breathing at night (possible sleep apnoea)
  • New or rapidly worsening night pain, night sweats, fever or weight loss
  • Low mood, worry or hopelessness alongside poor sleep
  • You think a medicine is affecting your sleep

Newly diagnosed and still working out a routine? Start with our newly diagnosed guide. If daily living is heavily limited by pain and poor sleep, the Benefits & PIP hub explains what support may be available.

Frequently asked questions

Are sleeping tablets a good idea?

The NHS generally suggests trying sleep habits and CBT-I first. Sleeping tablets are usually short-term only and can raise the risk of falls in older people. Talk to your GP before starting any.

Should I nap?

A short rest of 20–30 minutes in the early afternoon is fine for many people. Long or late naps tend to make nights worse.

Why is my arthritis worse in the morning?

Joints often stiffen when still. Morning stiffness lasting more than about 30 minutes, with swelling, can be a sign of inflammatory arthritis and is worth raising with your GP.
